input: In this process, liquid-liquid extraction is used to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of the acetic acid, expressed as the ratio of the concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase, is 1.83 at 25 °C, and the design provides for 7 countercurrent stages. The predicted recovery amounts to 94% of the acetic acid contained in the feed. The benefit of the countercurrent arrangement is that the aqueous phase, as it becomes progressively depleted in acid while passing through the cascade, is ultimately brought into contact with fresh solvent that retains a full capacity to take up acid even at the low concentrations involved, so that the driving force for transfer is maintained along the length of the cascade. The seven stages divide the overall separation into a series of steps, each of which brings the phases part of the way towards the final result at the stated distribution coefficient. Two assumptions underlie the prediction and should be clearly recognised. The stages are assumed to be equilibrium stages, so that the phases leaving each stage are taken to have reached equilibrium with one another. Mutual solubility between the two phases is also assumed to be negligible, so that neither phase flow is significantly altered by dissolution of the other phase. Neither assumption has been checked against the actual solvents to be used. Should the stages fall short of equilibrium, or should mutual solubility prove appreciable, the recovery achieved in practice would be lower than 94%, and confirmation by experiment on the real solvents would be needed.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous feed into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetic acid, taken as the concentration in the organic phase over the concentration in the aqueous phase, is 1.83 at 25 °C. The design uses 7 countercurrent stages. The predicted recovery is 94% of the acetic acid in the feed. The cascade works against the fall in driving force that a single contact would suffer: the aqueous phase gives up acid as it passes along the stages, and countercurrent flow brings it at the end against fresh solvent, which can still take up acid at the low concentration the raffinate has reached. Seven stages divide the separation into steps small enough that the stated recovery is reached at the stated distribution coefficient. The solvent leaves the cascade loaded with the recovered acid and is separated from it before reuse, and the raffinate leaves with the acid the cascade did not take. The solvent rate is the remaining design handle: it is set so that the aqueous phase is nowhere close to saturation against the solvent it meets, which keeps the coefficient the design uses valid along the whole cascade. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: the two phases leaving each stage are taken to be in equilibrium with each other. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so neither phase flow is changed by the other dissolving in it, and the solvent enters each stage carrying nothing but what the contact itself transfers. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A stage that falls short of equilibrium delivers less transfer than the prediction credits to it, and mutual solubility alters both phase flows and the concentrations on which the coefficient is based. The 94% is therefore the prediction for the ideal cascade, and the recovery on the actual solvents stands or falls with the two assumptions it rests on.
